warmup.q: On JDK 25, a virtual thread runs synchronized (cache) { rate = fxApi.fetch(pair); }, where fetch is an 80 ms HTTP call. What happens to its carrier thread during those 80 ms?
options: It is pinned: the carrier blocks for 80 ms, because synchronized always pins a virtual thread
It is free: since JDK 24 the virtual thread unmounts while it waits, even inside synchronized
The JVM throws, because blocking inside synchronized is not allowed on a virtual thread
The JVM converts the virtual thread into a platform thread for the duration of the block
warmup.why: JDK 24 (JEP 491) changed how monitors work, so a virtual thread can hold a monitor and still unmount. "synchronized pins" was true on JDK 21 to 23, and a lot of articles from that time still say it. The lock still serializes the callers, though: only one of them can fetch at a time.

sections.h: Pinning: when a virtual thread can't let go
sections.html:
A virtual thread is pinned when it reaches a blocking call but can't unmount. It stays on its carrier, and the carrier blocks with it. For that time the carrier is a plain platform thread again, and you have one carrier fewer for everybody else.

On JDK 21 to 23 the most common cause is a monitor. The JVM tracked monitor ownership per OS thread, so a virtual thread holding a synchronized lock could not leave its carrier. Here is the shape that hurts, from this lesson's lab:

Java
public synchronized BigDecimal rate(String pair) {   // a monitor
    BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair);
    if (r == null) {
        r = ratesService.fetch(pair);   // 100 ms socket read while holding the monitor
        rates.put(pair, r);
    }
    return r;
}
Kotlin
@Synchronized                                     // a monitor, exactly like Java's synchronized
fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal =
    rates.getOrPut(pair) { ratesService.fetch(pair) }   // 100 ms socket read while holding the monitor

On JDK 21 the thread holding the monitor pins its carrier for 100 ms. Every other caller that blocks trying to enter the monitor pins its carrier too. With 4 carriers, 4 waiting callers are enough to stop every virtual thread in the JVM, including requests that never touch the cache.

It can get worse than slow. In 2024 Netflix described services on Java 21 that stopped answering completely. Every carrier was held by a virtual thread pinned in synchronized code, waiting for a lock. The virtual thread that had to run next to move things along was unmounted, waiting for a free carrier, and there never was one. The figure shows the shape.

JDK 24 fixed this (JEP 491). Monitors were reworked so that a virtual thread can acquire, hold and release them independently of its carrier. synchronized and Object.wait() now unmount like ReentrantLock does. JDK 25 is the first long-term-support (LTS) release with the fix.

So the advice depends on your JDK. On JDK 25, leave working synchronized code alone. On JDK 21, replace synchronized around blocking calls with a ReentrantLock, which has always parked virtual threads properly. That is the first half of the lab.

try.title: Pin the only carrier
steps: Read PinningDemo. It runs with one carrier. A ticker wants to tick every 50 ms, while three virtual threads each block for 100 ms: inside synchronized, inside a ReentrantLock, or inside a class initializer.
Check your JDK with java -version. Predict the longest gap between ticks and the number of pinned events for each scenario on that JDK.
Run it. If you have both JDK 21 and JDK 25 installed, run it on both (point JAVA_HOME at each).

code.title: PinningDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l04; import jdk.jfr.Recording; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * One carrier thread, a ticker virtual thread that wants to tick every 50 ms, and three virtual * threads that each block for 100 ms in a different way. A pinned virtual thread blocks the only * carrier, so the ticker misses its ticks. JFR counts the pins. * * <p>Args: sync, lock or init to run one scenario (default: all three). */ public class PinningDemo { static final Object MONITOR = new Object(); static final ReentrantLock LOCK = new ReentrantLock(); // a class whose static initializer blocks, like one that loads config over the network static class SlowRatesTable { static final boolean READY; static { sleep(200); READY = true; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.setProperty("jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism", "1"); // one carrier makes pins easy to see System.out.println("JDK " + Runtime.version() + ", 1 carrier thread"); String only = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "all"; if (only.equals("all") || only.equals("sync")) run("synchronized + sleep", () -> { synchronized (MONITOR) { sleep(100); } }); if (only.equals("all") || only.equals("lock")) run("ReentrantLock + sleep", () -> { LOCK.lock(); try { sleep(100); } finally { LOCK.unlock(); } }); if (only.equals("all") || only.equals("init")) run("class init that sleeps", () -> { boolean ready = SlowRatesTable.READY; }); } static void run(String label, Runnable blocker) throws Exception { Path file = Files.createTempFile("pinning", ".jfr"); try (Recording rec = new Recording()) { rec.enable("jdk.VirtualThreadPinned").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(20)); rec.start(); List<Long> ticks = new ArrayList<>(); Thread ticker = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { ticks.add(System.nanoTime()); sleep(50); } }); sleep(10); List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) workers.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(blocker)); for (Thread w : workers) w.join(); ticker.join(); rec.stop(); rec.dump(file); long maxGap = 0; for (int i = 1; i < ticks.size(); i++) maxGap = Math.max(maxGap, (ticks.get(i) - ticks.get(i - 1)) / 1_000_000); List<RecordedEvent> pins = RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file).stream() .filter(e -> e.getEventType().getName().equals("jdk.VirtualThreadPinned")) // other recordings may add events .toList(); System.out.printf("%-24s longest gap between ticks: %3d ms pinned events: %d%n", label, maxGap, pins.size()); if (!pins.isEmpty() && pins.get(0).hasField("pinnedReason")) { // JDK 25 records a reason; JDK 21 only the stack System.out.println(" reason: " + pins.get(0).getString("pinnedReason")); } } finally { Files.deleteIfExists(file); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.html: package workbench.vthreads.l04 import jdk.jfr.Recording import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile import java.nio.file.Files import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.withLock /** * One carrier thread, a ticker virtual thread that wants to tick every 50 ms, and three virtual * threads that each block for 100 ms in a different way. A pinned virtual thread blocks the only * carrier, so the ticker misses its ticks. JFR counts the pins. * * Args: sync, lock or init to run one scenario (default: all three). */ private val monitor = Any() private val lock = ReentrantLock() // an object whose initializer blocks, like one that loads config over the network private object SlowFeeTable { val ready: Boolean init { Thread.sleep(200) ready = true } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { System.setProperty("jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism", "1") // one carrier makes pins easy to see println("JDK ${Runtime.version()}, 1 carrier thread") val only = args.getOrNull(0) ?: "all" // Kotlin's synchronized() is a monitor, exactly like Java's synchronized block if (only == "all" || only == "sync") runScenario("synchronized + sleep") { synchronized(monitor) { Thread.sleep(100) } } if (only == "all" || only == "lock") runScenario("ReentrantLock + sleep") { lock.withLock { Thread.sleep(100) } } if (only == "all" || only == "init") runScenario("object init that sleeps") { SlowFeeTable.ready } } private fun runScenario(label: String, blocker: () -> Unit) { val file = Files.createTempFile("pinning", ".jfr") try { Recording().use { rec -> rec.enable("jdk.VirtualThreadPinned").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(20)) rec.start() val ticks = mutableListOf<Long>() val ticker = Thread.ofVirtual().start { repeat(8) { ticks += System.nanoTime() Thread.sleep(50) } } Thread.sleep(10) val workers = List(3) { Thread.ofVirtual().start(blocker) } workers.forEach { it.join() } ticker.join() rec.stop() rec.dump(file) val maxGap = ticks.zipWithNext { a, b -> (b - a) / 1_000_000 }.max() val pins = RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file) .filter { it.eventType.name == "jdk.VirtualThreadPinned" } // other recordings may add events println("%-24s longest gap between ticks: %3d ms pinned events: %d".format(label, maxGap, pins.size)) pins.firstOrNull()?.takeIf { it.hasField("pinnedReason") }?.let { // JDK 25 records a reason; JDK 21 only the stack println(" reason: ${it.getString("pinnedReason")}") } } } finally { Files.deleteIfExists(file) } }

try.expect: On JDK 21: synchronized leaves a gap of about 300 ms between ticks and 3 pinned events (the three sleepers run one after another on the only carrier, and nothing else runs). ReentrantLock keeps the ticker at about 50 ms with 0 events. On JDK 25 synchronized behaves like ReentrantLock: about 50 ms, 0 events. The class initializer pins on both JDKs: a gap of about 200 ms and 1 event, and on JDK 25 JFR even names the reason (VM call to ...SlowRatesTable.<clinit> on stack).

sections.h: What still pins on JDK 25, and how to see it
sections.html:
JEP 491 removed the big case. Two smaller ones remain:

  • Native frames. If a virtual thread calls native code (a JNI method, or a downcall through the Foreign Function and Memory API), and that native code calls back into Java code that blocks, the virtual thread is pinned. The JVM can't move native frames to the heap.
  • Class initializers. A virtual thread that blocks while running a static {} block (or a Kotlin object's init) is pinned, because the JVM runs class initialization through its own frames.

The second one is easy to write by accident:

Java
class FeeTable {
    // runs inside <clinit>: an HTTP call here pins the first virtual thread that touches FeeTable
    static final Map<String, BigDecimal> FEES = loadFromConfigService();
}
Kotlin
object FeeTable {
    // runs inside <clinit>: an HTTP call here pins the first virtual thread that touches FeeTable
    val fees: Map<String, BigDecimal> = loadFromConfigService()
}

Move slow loading out of static initialization, into an explicit startup step or a lazily filled cache.

File I/O is a related case that isn't called pinning. A file read blocks inside the OS, so the virtual thread keeps its carrier, and the scheduler adds a temporary carrier to make up for it.

To find pinning, use JFR. The jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event is on by default in both built-in settings files, with a 20 ms threshold, and it records the stack of the pinned thread. On JDK 25 it also records the reason, the blocking operation and the carrier.

java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=pin.jfr,settings=profile -jar payments.jar
jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned pin.jfr

In a running service, jcmd <pid> JFR.start settings=profile does the same. To catch shorter pins, add jdk.VirtualThreadPinned#threshold=5ms to the -XX:StartFlightRecording options.

You'll find older advice to use -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full. That property worked on JDK 21 to 23 and was removed in JDK 24. On JDK 25 it is silently ignored, so a clean run with it proves nothing.

try.title: Read a pinned event
steps: Run PinningDemo once through Gradle (previous Try it) so its class is compiled.
From labs/, run the class initializer scenario with a JFR recording, then print the pinned events with the commands below.
Find the stack frame that names SlowRatesTable. On JDK 25, also read the pinnedReason and carrierThread fields.

code.title: terminal
code.html: java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=pin.jfr,settings=profile \ -cp vthreads/build/classes/java/demo workbench.vthreads.l04.PinningDemo init jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned pin.jfr

try.expect: One jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event of about 200 ms. Its stack shows Thread.sleep called from the static initializer of PinningDemo$SlowRatesTable. On JDK 25 the event also says blockingOperation = "LockSupport.park", pinnedReason = "VM call to ...SlowRatesTable.<clinit> on stack" and which ForkJoinPool-1-worker was blocked. On JDK 21 you only get the stack, which is still enough.

sections.html:
ThreadLocal works on virtual threads. Each virtual thread has its own values, exactly like a platform thread. The trap is a ThreadLocal used as a cache:

Java
// SimpleDateFormat isn't thread-safe, so keep one per thread
static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> FORMAT =
        ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'"));
Kotlin
// SimpleDateFormat isn't thread-safe, so keep one per thread
val FORMAT: ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> =
    ThreadLocal.withInitial { SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'") }

On a pool of 200 platform threads this builds 200 formatters, once, and reuses them for millions of requests. With one virtual thread per request, every request is a new thread with an empty map. The "cache" builds a formatter, uses it once, and throws it away. A million requests now build a million formatters. Nothing fails. You see it as allocation and GC time.

Per-thread buffers are worse, because they cost memory for as long as the thread lives. A 64 KB ThreadLocal<byte[]> scratch buffer was 13 MB on 200 threads. On 100,000 live virtual threads it is 6.4 GB.

The fixes are ordinary:

  • Use an immutable, thread-safe object and share it. DateTimeFormatter replaces SimpleDateFormat. This is the second half of the lab.
  • If the object is expensive and not thread-safe, use a real cache or pool for that object (a ConcurrentHashMap, a small object pool), not one per thread.
  • If it is cheap, just create it where you need it.

ThreadLocal for request context (an MDC entry, a tenant id) still works within one virtual thread, but it doesn't flow into threads you start, and it never gets wiped unless you call remove(). Scoped values, final in JDK 25, are the cleaner tool for that, and lesson 5 of this track covers them.

To find thread-local use in a migrated service, run it with -Djdk.traceVirtualThreadLocals=true. That is an unsupported diagnostic property, but it exists on JDK 21 and 25, and it prints a stack trace whenever a virtual thread sets a thread local.

try.title: Count the formatters
steps: Read ThreadLocalCostDemo. It formats 100,000 timestamps with a ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> on a pool of 8 platform threads, then with one virtual thread per task, then with one shared DateTimeFormatter.
Predict the three "formatters built" numbers before you run it.
Run it, and compare the times too.

code.title: ThreadLocalCostDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l04; import java.text.SimpleDateFormat; import java.time.Instant; import java.time.ZoneOffset; import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter; import java.util.Date; import java.util.TimeZone; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.LongFunction; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** * Formats 100,000 receipt timestamps three ways and counts how many formatter objects get built: * a ThreadLocal cache on a pool of 8 platform threads, the same cache with one virtual thread per * task, and one shared immutable DateTimeFormatter. */ public class ThreadLocalCostDemo { static final int TASKS = 100_000; static final AtomicInteger built = new AtomicInteger(); // the classic "SimpleDateFormat isn't thread-safe, so keep one per thread" cache static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> PER_THREAD = ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> { built.incrementAndGet(); SimpleDateFormat f = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'"); f.setTimeZone(TimeZone.getTimeZone("UTC")); return f; }); public static void main(String[] args) { run("ThreadLocal cache, pool of 8 platform threads", Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8), () -> t -> PER_THREAD.get().format(new Date(t))); run("ThreadLocal cache, virtual thread per task", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), () -> t -> PER_THREAD.get().format(new Date(t))); run("shared DateTimeFormatter, virtual threads", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), () -> { built.incrementAndGet(); // built once, here, and shared by every thread DateTimeFormatter shared = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'").withZone(ZoneOffset.UTC); return t -> shared.format(Instant.ofEpochMilli(t)); }); } static void run(String label, ExecutorService executor, Supplier<LongFunction<String>> setup) { int before = built.get(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); LongFunction<String> stamp = setup.get(); try (executor) { for (int i = 0; i < TASKS; i++) { long t = 1_700_000_000_000L + i; executor.execute(() -> stamp.apply(t)); } } System.out.printf("%-46s formatters built: %,7d time: %,5d ms%n", label, built.get() - before, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } }

before, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) }

try.expect: 8, then 100,000, then 1. The pool built one formatter per thread and reused it. With virtual threads every task built its own and threw it away. The shared DateTimeFormatter is also the fastest line (one run here: 958 ms, 1,074 ms and 253 ms), though times swing a lot on a busy machine.

sections.html:
Virtual threads make waiting cheap. They do nothing for computing. There are as many carriers as cores, so at most that many virtual threads compute at once, which is exactly what a fixed pool of that size gives you.

It is worse than "no gain", because there is no time slicing. A virtual thread that signs a large settlement batch for 3 seconds keeps its carrier for 3 seconds. Put four of those on a 4-core pod, and every HTTP request handled on virtual threads waits until one of them finishes, even requests that only need a millisecond of CPU.

Keep heavy CPU work on a bounded pool of platform threads, and let the virtual thread wait for it:

Java
private final ExecutorService cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors());

Receipt settle(Batch b) throws Exception {
    Signature sig = cpu.submit(() -> signer.sign(b)).get();   // heavy CPU on a bounded platform pool
    return ledger.record(b, sig);                              // blocking I/O stays on the virtual thread
}
Kotlin
private val cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors())

fun settle(b: Batch): Receipt {
    val sig = cpu.submit(Callable { signer.sign(b) }).get()   // heavy CPU on a bounded platform pool
    return ledger.record(b, sig)                              // blocking I/O stays on the virtual thread
}

The virtual thread parks in get(), so it holds no carrier while the signing runs. The CPU pool keeps the heavy work to its own threads, and the OS time-slices those threads against the carriers, so request handling keeps moving.

The line is fuzzy for work that is a little of both. Parsing a 2 KB JSON body is fine on a virtual thread. Anything that runs for tens of milliseconds without blocking (hashing, compression, PDF rendering, big XML transforms) belongs on the CPU pool.

try.title: Hash on virtual threads
steps: Read CpuBoundDemo. Each of 64 tasks hashes a 1 MB buffer 20 times: a fixed amount of pure CPU work.
Predict which line finishes first: a pool sized to your cores, or one virtual thread per task.
Run it, then run -Pargs='256 20' and predict again.

code.title: CpuBoundDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.vthreads.l04; import java.security.MessageDigest; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** * 64 CPU-bound tasks (each hashes the same 1 MB buffer many times, a fixed amount of work) * on a pool sized to the cores, then with one virtual thread per task. * * <p>Args: number of tasks, hash rounds per task. Default: 64 20. */ public class CpuBoundDemo { static final byte[] DATA = new byte[1 << 20]; public static void main(String[] args) { int tasks = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 64; int rounds = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 20; int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(); Runnable work = () -> hash(rounds); hash(rounds); // warm up the JIT once time("fixed pool of " + cores + " platform threads", Executors.newFixedThreadPool(cores), tasks, work); time("virtual thread per task", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), tasks, work); } static void time(String label, ExecutorService executor, int tasks, Runnable work) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (executor) { for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) executor.execute(work); } System.out.printf("%-34s %d tasks in %,5d ms%n", label, tasks, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } static byte[] hash(int rounds) { try { MessageDigest sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256"); byte[] out = null; for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++) out = sha.digest(DATA); // pure CPU, never blocks return out; } catch (Exception e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); } } }

alt.title: CpuBoundDemo.kt

Default: 64 20. */ private val data = ByteArray(1 shl 20) fun main(args: Array<String>) { val tasks = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 64 val rounds = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 20 val cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() val work = Runnable { hashRounds(rounds) } hashRounds(rounds) // warm up the JIT once timeTasks("fixed pool of $cores platform threads", Executors.newFixedThreadPool(cores), tasks, work) timeTasks("virtual thread per task", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), tasks, work) } private fun timeTasks(label: String, executor: ExecutorService, tasks: Int, work: Runnable) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() executor.use { exec -> repeat(tasks) { exec.execute(work) } } println("%-34s %d tasks in %,5d ms".format(label, tasks, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } private fun hashRounds(rounds: Int): ByteArray { val sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256") var out = ByteArray(0) repeat(rounds) { out = sha.digest(data) } // pure CPU, never blocks return out }

try.expect: Both lines take about the same time (around 1 s on 4 cores in one run here), and the virtual thread line is never meaningfully faster. On a busy machine it can even be slower. Four times the tasks take about four times as long on both. The work is limited by cores, and both setups use all of them.

analogy: Back to the office from the lesson on carriers: desks are carriers, and workers pack their papers into a briefcase and free the desk whenever they wait. Pinning is a worker who is handcuffed to the desk while waiting. On JDK 21 to 23, holding a synchronized lock was such a handcuff, and a few handcuffed workers waiting on each other could block every desk in the building. JDK 24 removed that handcuff. A ThreadLocal cache is a drawer in the desk that each worker fills with their own stationery: fine when the same 200 people work there every day, useless when every visitor is new. The analogy breaks for CPU work: a worker who is busy at the desk is not stuck, they are working. They just never get up, because nobody tells them to.
world: If your Quarkus services still run on JDK 21, check before you turn on @RunOnVirtualThread: JDBC drivers, HTTP clients and logging appenders that use synchronized around socket I/O pin on JDK 21 to 23. Many libraries have since switched to ReentrantLock, but trust a JFR recording under load more than a changelog. On JDK 25 that whole class of problem is gone, which is the best argument for upgrading first. The ThreadLocal trap applies on every JDK: look for ThreadLocal.withInitial caches of formatters, MessageDigest, Cipher or buffers in payment code, and for CPU-heavy steps such as signing settlement files or generating statements, which belong on a bounded platform pool.
mistake: The most common mistake today is following advice written for JDK 21 on JDK 25. Teams rewrite every synchronized block in the codebase as ReentrantLock, which is churn with no benefit on JDK 24 and later, and they "check" for pinning with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full, which JDK 24 removed, so it prints nothing and looks like a clean bill of health. Know which JDK you run. On JDK 25, keep synchronized, keep a JFR recording with jdk.VirtualThreadPinned in staging and production, and fix the pins it actually reports, which are mostly slow static initializers and native code.

compare.title: Taking the monitor out of the slow path

java.title: Java: synchronized becomes ReentrantLock
java.html: // JDK 21 to 23: this pins for the whole fetch public synchronized BigDecimal rate(String pair) { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, ratesService::fetch); } // any JDK: a j.u.c lock parks a waiting virtual thread instead private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); public BigDecimal rate(String pair) { lock.lock(); try { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, ratesService::fetch); // rates is a plain HashMap } finally { lock.unlock(); } }

kotlin.title: Kotlin: @Synchronized becomes withLock
kotlin.html: // JDK 21 to 23: @Synchronized and synchronized(lock) {} are monitors, and pin the same way @Synchronized fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = rates.getOrPut(pair) { ratesService.fetch(pair) } // any JDK: kotlin.concurrent.withLock does lock / try / finally / unlock for you private val lock = ReentrantLock() fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = lock.withLock { rates.getOrPut(pair) { ratesService.fetch(pair) } // rates is a plain HashMap }

compare.note: Kotlin has no synchronized keyword, but @Synchronized and the synchronized(lock) { } function both compile to the same JVM monitor instructions as Java, so they pin on JDK 21 to 23 in exactly the same way. The Kotlin fix is shorter, because the standard library's withLock extension writes the lock(), try and finally { unlock() } for you, and it is inline, so it costs nothing. Note what neither version does: it doesn't let two different pairs load in parallel. That needs a lock per key, and on JDK 25 it is the only reason left to change this code.

worked.title: Find and fix a pin from a JFR recording (JDK 21)

steps.say: The quote service runs on JDK 21 with virtual threads. Under load, p99 latency jumps from 150 ms to several seconds while CPU stays low. Record a few minutes of the load test with JFR and print the pinned events.
steps.code: jcmd $(pgrep -f quote-service) JFR.start name=pins settings=profile duration=120s filename=pins.jfr jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned pins.jfr | head -40

steps.say: Read the stack in the event. The pin lasts as long as the FX call, and the frame just above the blocking call is a synchronized method of your cache.
Replace the monitor with a ReentrantLock, keeping the same "load once" behavior. The lock still serializes loads, but a waiting virtual thread now parks and frees its carrier.
steps.code: private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); public BigDecimal rate(String pair) { lock.lock(); // 1. take the lock (parks, doesn't pin) try { BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair); if (r == null) { r = ratesService.fetch(pair); // 2. slow call: the thread can unmount here rates.put(pair, r); } return r; } finally { lock.unlock(); // 3. always release } }

alt.html: private val lock = ReentrantLock() fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = lock.withLock { // 1. take the lock (parks, doesn't pin) rates[pair] ?: ratesService.fetch(pair) // 2. slow call: the thread can unmount here .also { rates[pair] = it } } // 3. withLock always releases

steps.say: Verify with the same recording under the same load: zero jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events from FxRateCache, and p99 back near 150 ms. Then put the JDK 25 upgrade on the plan, so the next synchronized in a library doesn't need the same fix.

lab.title: Unpin a cache and retire a ThreadLocal
steps: Run the tests once. Three fail: the monitor check, the JFR pinning check (on JDK 21 to 23; on JDK 24+ it passes even now, which is the point of JEP 491) and the formatter count.
In FxRateCache, remove both synchronized modifiers and add a private final ReentrantLock lock. Wrap the bodies of rate and size in lock.lock(); try { ... } finally { lock.unlock(); }.

Read the JFR test in TrapsTest. It records jdk.VirtualThreadPinned while four virtual threads load four pairs, then asserts the recording is empty. You can use the same few lines in your own services' tests.

In ReceiptStamp, replace the ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> with one static final DateTimeFormatter, built once with .withZone(ZoneOffset.UTC). Count it in BUILT when you build it, and format with FORMAT.format(Instant.ofEpochMilli(epochMillis)).
Run the tests until all six pass.
hints: The monitor test calls Thread.holdsLock(cache) from inside the rates service. That returns true only for a synchronized monitor on the cache object, never for a ReentrantLock.
Don't drop the lock entirely: the load-once test sends 100 virtual threads at the same pair and expects exactly one call to the rates service.
DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'") needs a zone to format an Instant; without withZone you get an UnsupportedTemporalTypeException.

drill.title: Unpin a method from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Rewrite this method for a JDK 21 service so it never holds a monitor during the call, without changing what it does: synchronized Token refresh() { if (token.expired()) token = authServer.fetchToken(); return token; }. Then say in one sentence whether you would still change it on JDK 25.

answer.html: private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); Token refresh() { lock.lock(); // outside the try try { if (token.expired()) token = authServer.fetchToken(); // may block: parks, doesn't pin return token; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } // On JDK 25: no need. synchronized no longer pins (JEP 491), so the original is fine.

alt.html: private val lock = ReentrantLock() fun refresh(): Token = lock.withLock { // lock, try, finally unlock if (token.expired()) token = authServer.fetchToken() // may block: parks, doesn't pin token } // On JDK 25: no need. @Synchronized no longer pins (JEP 491), so the original is fine.

recap: A pinned virtual thread can't unmount at a blocking call, so its carrier blocks with it.
On JDK 21 to 23, blocking while holding a monitor (synchronized, @Synchronized, Object.wait) pins. JDK 24 (JEP 491) fixed that, and JDK 25 is the first LTS with the fix.
On JDK 25, blocking inside a class initializer or under a native frame still pins. File I/O captures the carrier, and the scheduler compensates.
Find pins with the JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned (on by default, 20 ms threshold). -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads was removed in JDK 24.
A ThreadLocal cache builds one object per virtual thread, which means one per task. Share an immutable object such as DateTimeFormatter instead.
CPU-bound work gains nothing and, with no time slicing, can starve other virtual threads. Run it on a bounded platform pool.

explain.prompt: Your team lead read a 2023 article and wants to ban synchronized before the move to virtual threads. The service runs on JDK 25. Explain what pinning is, whether the ban helps, and what you would check instead.
explain.answer: Pinning is when a virtual thread can't unmount at a blocking call, so it keeps its carrier and the carrier blocks with it. On JDK 21 to 23, holding a synchronized monitor while blocking caused it, and a few pinned threads could block every carrier. JDK 24 fixed that with JEP 491, so on JDK 25 a ban on synchronized changes nothing for pinning and just churns code. What still pins on JDK 25 is blocking inside a class initializer or under native code, so I'd keep a JFR recording with jdk.VirtualThreadPinned running in staging and production and fix what it reports. I'd also check the traps that have nothing to do with pinning: ThreadLocal caches that now build an object per request, and CPU-heavy steps that should stay on a bounded platform pool.

deeper.html:
Why monitors pinned in the first place. Before JDK 24, HotSpot recorded the owner of a monitor as the OS thread that held it. If a virtual thread could unmount while holding a monitor, another virtual thread mounted on the same carrier would appear to own it too. Rather than redesign monitors for JDK 21, the Loom team shipped with pinning and a warning. JEP 491 changed the JVM to record the virtual thread as the owner, so the thread can move freely.

Object.wait() on JDK 21. A virtual thread in Object.wait() was pinned too, but the scheduler compensated by adding a temporary carrier, up to jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize. That kept wait-heavy code alive at the cost of extra OS threads. Blocking on monitor entry got no such help, which is why the deadlock in this lesson's figure was possible.

Testing for pins. The lab's JFR test is a pattern you can copy into a service's integration tests: start a jdk.jfr.Recording with jdk.VirtualThreadPinned enabled, run a realistic slice of traffic on virtual threads, stop and dump the recording, and assert there are no events. Warm up first, so one-time class loading doesn't show up as a pin. On JDK 24 and later, such a test catches class initializer and native pins. On JDK 21, it also catches every synchronized around I/O.

Inheritable thread locals. A new thread copies its parent's InheritableThreadLocal values by default, and that includes virtual threads. Creating a million virtual threads from a thread with large inheritable values copies them a million times. Thread.ofVirtual().inheritInheritableThreadLocals(false) turns the copy off for threads that don't need it.
